"Against All Odds (Take a Look at Me Now)" (also titled "Against All Odds") is a song by English singer and songwriter Phil Collins recorded for the soundtrack to the 1984 film of the same name. The song is a power ballad in which its protagonist implores an ex-lover to "take a look at me now", knowing that reconciliation is "against all odds", but worth the gamble. The single reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in the United States, the first of seven for Collins in his solo career. It also topped the charts in Canada, Ireland, and Norway, while peaking at number two on the UK singles chart.

The song has been covered by several singers with some versions of which have been successful in both the US and UK markets. It has twice reached number one in the UK with the pairing of Mariah Carey and pop group Westlife in September 2000, and then by Steve Brookstein, the first winner of The X Factor, in January 2005.

sections.heading: Background and development
Reception
sections.wikitext:
"Against All Odds" won the [[Grammy Award]] for [[Grammy Award for Best Male Pop Vocal Performance#Recipients|Best Pop Vocal Performance, Male]] in [[27th Annual Grammy Awards#Award winners|1985]], was nominated for [[Grammy Award for Song of the Year#Recipients|Song of the Year]] and for an [[57th Academy Awards#Awards|Academy Award]] as well as for a [[42nd Golden Globe Awards#Winners and nominees|Golden Globe]] both in the [[Golden Globe Award for Best Original Song#1980s|Best Original Song]] categories. At the Academy Awards ceremony, Collins was not invited to sing his song on stage and instead sat in the audience as dancer [[Ann Reinking]] gave a mostly lip-synced vocal performance accompanied by a dance routine. Reinking's performance was poorly received by critics from the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' and ''[[People (magazine)|People]]'',<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-03-31-ca-18761-story.html|title=Down The Academy|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|location=Los Angeles|date=31 March 1985|access-date=9 August 2015|archive-date=3 October 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151003182406/http://articles.latimes.com/1985-03-31/entertainment/ca-18761_1_oscar-academy-awards-phil-collins|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="people">{{cite web|url=http://www.people.com/people/archive/article/0,,20091234,00.html|title=Short, Pudgy and Bald, All Phil Collins Produces Is Hits|work=[[People (magazine)|People]]|first=Roger|last=Wolmuth|date=8 July 1985|access-date=9 August 2015|archive-date=24 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924081636/http://www.people.com/people/archive/article/0,,20091234,00.html|url-status=live}}</ref> as well as by Collins himself in a ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' interview.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/news/phil-collins-beats-the-odds-19850523|title=Phil Collins Beats The Odds|magazine=[[Rolling Stone]]|first=Rob|last=Hoerburger|date=23 May 1985|access-date=2 October 2015|archive-date=18 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171118222636/https://www.rollingstone.com/music/news/phil-collins-beats-the-odds-19850523|url-status=dead}}</ref>

When another song Collins performed for a film, "[[Separate Lives]]", was being nominated for an [[58th Academy Awards|Academy Award]], in interviews about the original snub by the Academy for "Against All Odds", Collins would jokingly say "the hell with him – I'm going up too", referring to what he would do if the Stephen Bishop-written song were to win the award.<ref name="Dallas">{{cite news|first=Stephen|last=Williams|title=A Phil Collins Special And 'Miami Vice' on Record|work=[[Newsday]]|date=4 October 1985}}</ref> Collins lost to the [[Stevie Wonder]] song "[[I Just Called to Say I Love You]]".

Writing for her review of the film soundtrack, [[AllMusic]]'s Heather Phares said that the film is best remembered for the inclusion of Collins' "classic theme song".<ref name="PharesAllRev">{{cite web|last=Phares|first=Heather|title=Against All Odds [Original Soundtrack]|url=http://www.allmusic.com/album/against-all-odds-original-soundtrack-r84169/review|work=Allmusic|publisher=Rovi Corporation|access-date=3 September 2011|archive-date=15 March 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110315044747/http://www.allmusic.com/album/against-all-odds-original-soundtrack-r84169/review|url-status=live}}</ref> Phares added that the song "remains not only one of Collins' definitive singles, but one of the 1980s' best love songs".<ref name="PharesAllRev" /> Hackford had the same view, stating that it "decidedly" helped the film: people identified the song with the film and came to watch it.{{sfn|Denisoff|Romanowski|1991|p=406}} When the single reached the top five, it contributed to the increased box office sales of the film.{{sfn|Denisoff|Romanowski|1991|p=406}}

Rapper [[RZA]] named "Against All Odds" as his favourite power ballad in an article on such songs in ''[[Spin (magazine)|Spin]]''.<ref>Aaron, Charles. "Don't Fight the Power". ''[[Spin (magazine)|Spin]]''. November 2001.</ref> ''[[The Guardian]]'' and ''[[American Songwriter]]'' both named it as Collins' second-best solo song behind "[[In the Air Tonight]]".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2020/aug/13/phil-collins-greatest-solo-songs-ranked|title=Phil Collins' greatest solo songs – ranked!|first=Michael|last=Hann|work=[[The Guardian]]|date=13 August 2020|access-date=6 April 2022|archive-date=6 April 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220406194659/https://www.theguardian.com/music/2020/aug/13/phil-collins-greatest-solo-songs-ranked|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://americansongwriter.com/top-10-phil-collins-solo-songs/|title=Top 10 Phil Collins Solo Songs|first=Tina|last=Benitez-Eves|work=[[American Songwriter]]|date=January 13, 2022|access-date=April 6, 2022|archive-date=6 April 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220406194659/https://americansongwriter.com/top-10-phil-collins-solo-songs/|url-status=live}}</ref>

"Against All Odds" won the Grammy Award for Best Pop Vocal Performance, Male in 1985, was nominated for Song of the Year and for an Academy Award as well as for a Golden Globe both in the Best Original Song categories. At the Academy Awards ceremony, Collins was not invited to sing his song on stage and instead sat in the audience as dancer Ann Reinking gave a mostly lip-synced vocal performance accompanied by a dance routine. Reinking's performance was poorly received by critics from the Los Angeles Times and People, as well as by Collins himself in a Rolling Stone interview.

When another song Collins performed for a film, "Separate Lives", was being nominated for an Academy Award, in interviews about the original snub by the Academy for "Against All Odds", Collins would jokingly say "the hell with him – I'm going up too", referring to what he would do if the Stephen Bishop-written song were to win the award. Collins lost to the Stevie Wonder song "I Just Called to Say I Love You".

Writing for her review of the film soundtrack, AllMusic's Heather Phares said that the film is best remembered for the inclusion of Collins' "classic theme song". Phares added that the song "remains not only one of Collins' definitive singles, but one of the 1980s' best love songs". Hackford had the same view, stating that it "decidedly" helped the film: people identified the song with the film and came to watch it.{{sfn|Denisoff|Romanowski|1991|p=406}} When the single reached the top five, it contributed to the increased box office sales of the film.{{sfn|Denisoff|Romanowski|1991|p=406}}

Rapper RZA named "Against All Odds" as his favourite power ballad in an article on such songs in Spin. The Guardian and American Songwriter both named it as Collins' second-best solo song behind "In the Air Tonight".

sections.heading: Commercial performance
sections.wikitext: "Against All Odds" became Collins' third top-ten single in the UK, peaking at #2 for three weeks in 1984. It was kept from the top spot by [[Lionel Richie]]'s "[[Hello (Lionel Richie song)|Hello]]" for the first of these three weeks, and [[Duran Duran]]'s "[[The Reflex]]" for the next two. It was ranked 14th in the year-end best-seller chart. In the U.S. and Canada, it peaked at No. 1 on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] charts for three weeks in the spring of 1984 and four weeks on the Canadian [[RPM (magazine)|RPM]] charts.<ref name="HoganAllInfo" /> ''Billboard'' ranked it as the No. 5 song for 1984 and ''[[RPM (magazine)|RPM]]'' ranked it at No. 2.<ref>[[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1984]]</ref>

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext:
The single's music video was directed by Taylor Hackford, produced by Jeffrey Abelson through Parallax Productions and cinematographed by [[Daniel Pearl (cinematographer)|Daniel Pearl]].<ref>{{cite web|author=Daniel Pearl|url=http://www.danielpearldp.com/page3.html|title=Resumé|access-date=14 September 2012|archive-date=18 September 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120918070848/http://www.danielpearldp.com/page3.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Hackford was paid [[United States Dollar|US$]]20,000 (out of a total budget of US$45,000)<ref name="Film History">{{cite journal|last1=Denisoff|first1=R. Serge|last2=Romanowski|first2=William D.|author-link2=William D. Romanowski|year=1990|title=Synergy in 1980s Film and Music: Formula for Success or Industry Mythology?|journal= Film History|volume=4|issue=3|pages=257–276, here p. 259|jstor=3815137}}</ref> for a complete Collins clip. The music video was released in February 1984.{{sfn|Denisoff|Romanowski|1991|p=406}} A No. 1 MTV video for several weeks, [[MTV]] ranked it as No. 4 four in its 1984 year-end top 20 video countdown.<ref name=mtv>{{cite web|url=http://www.platypuscomix.net/videos/toptwenty.html|title=Remember back when MTV used to be cool?|publisher=Platypus Comix|access-date=18 August 2006|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060901211150/http://www.platypuscomix.net/videos/toptwenty.html|archive-date=1 September 2006|url-status=dead}}</ref> Gary LeMel, music supervisor at Columbia, felt the music video on MTV increased ''Against All Odds''' box office takings by at least US$5 million.<ref name="Film History" />

The concept for the video was created by Keith Williams, a Welsh-born writer who had already worked with Abelson on the video for "[[Dancing with Myself]]" ([[Billy Idol]]), and who would go on to also create concepts for "[[Holding Out for a Hero]]" ([[Bonnie Tyler]]) and "[[Ghostbusters (song)|Ghostbusters]]" ([[Ray Parker Jr.]]) for the same producer as well as "[[Say You, Say Me]]" (Lionel Richie) from ''[[White Nights (1985 film)|White Nights]]'', which Hackford also directed.<ref>{{cite web|title=Keith Williams IMVDb|url=https://imvdb.com/n/keith-williams|website=IMVDb|access-date=17 November 2017|language=en|archive-date=18 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171118222003/https://imvdb.com/n/keith-williams|url-status=live}}</ref>

The music video is an early example of a highly conceptual approach to creating hybrid movie/music-videos that producer Abelson pioneered. Echoing the [[love triangle]] theme of the film, Collins is seen performing in front of a wall of rainwater that is alternately lit red, blue, and green—each colour representing one of the three main characters in the film. It is this colour schematic that is used as an organic segue to and from character-specific scenes in the movie. The final scene pulls back from Collins to reveal him standing in the middle of a water-filled triangle formed from [[Neon lamp|neon tubes]] in the same three colours—completing the visual concept as the three main characters are superimposed around the neon triangle's three sides.

The single's music video was directed by Taylor Hackford, produced by Jeffrey Abelson through Parallax Productions and cinematographed by Daniel Pearl. Hackford was paid US$20,000 (out of a total budget of US$45,000) for a complete Collins clip. The music video was released in February 1984.{{sfn|Denisoff|Romanowski|1991|p=406}} A No. 1 MTV video for several weeks, MTV ranked it as No. 4 four in its 1984 year-end top 20 video countdown. Gary LeMel, music supervisor at Columbia, felt the music video on MTV increased Against All Odds box office takings by at least US$5 million.

The concept for the video was created by Keith Williams, a Welsh-born writer who had already worked with Abelson on the video for "Dancing with Myself" (Billy Idol), and who would go on to also create concepts for "Holding Out for a Hero" (Bonnie Tyler) and "Ghostbusters" (Ray Parker Jr.) for the same producer as well as "Say You, Say Me" (Lionel Richie) from White Nights, which Hackford also directed.

The music video is an early example of a highly conceptual approach to creating hybrid movie/music-videos that producer Abelson pioneered. Echoing the love triangle theme of the film, Collins is seen performing in front of a wall of rainwater that is alternately lit red, blue, and green—each colour representing one of the three main characters in the film. It is this colour schematic that is used as an organic segue to and from character-specific scenes in the movie. The final scene pulls back from Collins to reveal him standing in the middle of a water-filled triangle formed from neon tubes in the same three colours—completing the visual concept as the three main characters are superimposed around the neon triangle's three sides.

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext:
"Against All Odds (Take a Look at Me Now)" received positive reviews. Danyel Smith of ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' wrote: "Listeners with an eye on the tabloids could read her close, ringing interpretation of [[Phil Collins]]' 1984 hit, 'Against All Odds (Take a Look at Me Now)', as a postmortem on her bittersweet affair with Yankee shortstop [[Derek Jeter]] and a poignant evocation of the couple's shared mixed-race heritage ('You're the only one who really knew me at all')."<ref>{{cite news|date=November 12, 1999|title=Rainbow Review {{!}} Music Reviews and News|publisher=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|url=https://ew.com/article/1999/11/12/rainbow/|access-date=November 17, 2017|archive-date=18 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210518021311/https://ew.com/article/1999/11/12/rainbow/|url-status=live}}</ref> ''[[Los Angeles Times]]''<nowiki/>' Elysa Gardner called this cover "surprisingly faithful, forthright" and "she resists her tendency to over-embellish notes and focuses on what really matters: the melody and lyrics".<ref>{{cite news|last=Gardner|first=Elysa|date=October 31, 1999|title=Record Rack|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1999-oct-31-ca-28099-story.html|access-date=November 17, 2017|archive-date=18 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210518021311/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1999-oct-31-ca-28099-story.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[MTV (Asian TV channel)|MTV Asia]] editor Dara Cook wrote: "Mariah festoons herself in Phil Collins' 1980s melodic garb, appropriately pret a porter with overwrought emotion. She delicately ascends the sparely accompanied first verses—but alas, that damn drum roll soon sounds and the bouffant strings and vocal gymnastics ensue."<ref>{{cite web|last=Cook|first=Dara|title=Mariah Carey – Rainbow {{!}} Reviews {{!}} CD|url=http://web.mtvasia.com/Review/CD/C1999000115.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160113081939/http://web.mtvasia.com/Review/CD/C1999000115.html|archive-date=January 13, 2016|access-date=November 17, 2017|website=[[MTV (Asian TV channel)|MTV Asia]]|publisher=[[ViacomCBS Networks EMEAA|Viacom]]}}</ref> ''[[Rolling Stone]]''{{'}}s Arion Berger was not happy with the cover selection which he called a "drippy Eighties power-pop hit".<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Berger|first=Arion|date=November 25, 1999|title=Rainbow {{!}} Album Reviews|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/rainbow-190409/|url-status=live|access-date=November 17, 2017|magazine=[[Rolling Stone]]|archive-date=18 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210518021311/https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/rainbow-190409/}}</ref>

The song was released as the first single from the band's second album, ''[[Coast to Coast (Westlife album)|Coast to Coast]]'' (2000). The song was released on September 15, 2000.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/2000/Music-Week-2000-09-16.pdf|title=New Releases – For Week Starting September 18, 2000: Singles|magazine=[[Music Week]]|page=31|date=16 September 2000|access-date=4 August 2021|archive-date=4 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210804143412/https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/2000/Music-Week-2000-09-16.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> Carey's vocals from the solo version were retained for the duet, though a new instrumental track was produced by Carey and [[Steve Mac]], featuring a more organic sound with violins. The music video shows Carey and Westlife recording the song and exploring the island of [[Capri]] by boat.

The single debuted at number one in the United Kingdom, selling 112,000 copies.<ref name="MW 30 Sep">{{cite magazine|title=Single Factile|last=Jones|first=Alan|magazine=[[Music Week]]|page=17|date=30 September 2000}}</ref> It remained at number one in its second week, selling a further 78,500 copies.<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Chart Commentary|last=Jones|first=Alan|magazine=[[Music Week]]|page=15|date=7 October 2000}}</ref> The song became Carey's second to top the [[UK Singles Chart]] and Westlife's sixth consecutive number one.<ref name="MW 30 Sep" /> As of November 2021, the song has sold 507,000 copies in the country. It is Westlife's sixth biggest selling single (paid-for sales and combined sales categories) of all-time and their fifteenth most streamed single in the United Kingdom.<ref>{{cite web|last=Copsey|first=Rob|date=January 12, 2019|title=Westlife's Top 20 biggest songs on the Official Charts|url=https://www.officialcharts.com/chart-news/westlifes-top-20-biggest-songs-on-the-official-charts__25303/|url-status=live|access-date=January 17, 2019|publisher=[[Official Charts Company]]|archive-date=12 January 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190112200650/https://www.officialcharts.com/chart-news/westlifes-top-20-biggest-songs-on-the-official-charts__25303/}}</ref>

Its chart success in European countries led to its inclusion on the international editions of Carey's compilation albums ''[[Greatest Hits (Mariah Carey album)|Greatest Hits]]'' (2001) and ''[[Number 1 to Infinity|#1 to Infinity]]'' (2015).

sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext: In 2004, Brookstein won the televised UK talent competition ''The X Factor'', and recorded a cover of the [[Phil Collins]] 1984 hit "Against All Odds" as his debut single. It entered the [[UK Singles Chart]] at number two behind "[[Do They Know It's Christmas?]]" by [[Band Aid 20]], and then climbed to number one, where it stayed for one week from 2 January 2005 to 8 January 2005 and was replaced by [[Elvis Presley]]'s "[[Jailhouse Rock (song)|Jailhouse Rock]]". "Against All Odds" was later included on Brookstein's debut album ''[[Heart and Soul (Steve Brookstein album)|Heart and Soul]]''.
sections.text: In 2004, Brookstein won the televised UK talent competition The X Factor, and recorded a cover of the Phil Collins 1984 hit "Against All Odds" as his debut single. It entered the UK Singles Chart at number two behind "Do They Know It's Christmas?" by Band Aid 20, and then climbed to number one, where it stayed for one week from 2 January 2005 to 8 January 2005 and was replaced by Elvis Presley's "Jailhouse Rock". "Against All Odds" was later included on Brookstein's debut album Heart and Soul.

sections.heading: Chart performance
sections.wikitext: "Against All Odds" debuted at number two in the United Kingdom, behind [[Band Aid 20]]'s version of "[[Do They Know It's Christmas?#Band Aid 20|Do They Know It's Christmas?]]", and at number 11 in Ireland. It charted at number one in the UK the following week. "Against All Odds" sold 127,701 copies in its first week in the UK, the lowest first-week sales for an ''X Factor'' winner's single until 2015.<ref name="Little Mix">{{cite news|last=Plunkett|first=John|title=X Factor: Little Mix have lowest-selling winner's single since 2004|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/dec/19/x-factor-little-mix-cannonball|work=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=21 December 2011|date=19 December 2011|location=London|archive-date=10 May 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170510185438/https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/dec/19/x-factor-little-mix-cannonball|url-status=live}}</ref> Brookstein's version has sold 204,000 copies in the UK to date, making it the lowest-selling'' X Factor'' winner's single.<ref name="sales figures">{{cite web|url=http://www.officialcharts.com/chart-news/the-winner-takes-it-all-the-biggest-selling-x-factor-winners-singles-revealed__7770/|title=The biggest selling X Factor winner's singles revealed|last=Myers|first=Justin|date=9 December 2015|publisher=[[Official Charts Company]]|access-date=16 December 2015|archive-date=18 December 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151218034147/http://www.officialcharts.com/chart-news/the-winner-takes-it-all-the-biggest-selling-x-factor-winners-singles-revealed__7770/|url-status=live}}</ref> It has sold fewer than half the copies of [[Leon Jackson]]'s "[[When You Believe (Leon Jackson song)|When You Believe]]" and [[Little Mix]]'s "[[Cannonball (Little Mix song)|Cannonball]]", a third of [[Joe McElderry]]'s "[[The Climb (Miley Cyrus song)#Joe McElderry version|The Climb]]", a quarter of [[Leona Lewis]]'s "[[A Moment Like This (Leona Lewis song)|A Moment Like This]]", and a fifth of those of [[Matt Cardle]]'s "[[When We Collide]]", [[Shayne Ward]]'s "[[That's My Goal]]", [[James Arthur (singer)|James Arthur]]'s "[[Impossible (James Arthur song)|Impossible]]" and [[Alexandra Burke]]'s "[[Hallelujah (Alexandra Burke song)|Hallelujah]]". The next fewest sales from a winner's song was [[Sam Bailey]]'s version of "[[Skyscraper (Sam Bailey song)|Skyscraper]]", which had first-week sales of 149,000 copies, 26,000 more than "Against All Odds".<ref name="sales figures" /> However, Louisa Johnson, Matt Terry and Rak Su would all have lower first week sales in later years.
sections.text: "Against All Odds" debuted at number two in the United Kingdom, behind Band Aid 20's version of "Do They Know It's Christmas?", and at number 11 in Ireland. It charted at number one in the UK the following week. "Against All Odds" sold 127,701 copies in its first week in the UK, the lowest first-week sales for an X Factor winner's single until 2015. Brookstein's version has sold 204,000 copies in the UK to date, making it the lowest-selling X Factor winner's single. It has sold fewer than half the copies of Leon Jackson's "When You Believe" and Little Mix's "Cannonball", a third of Joe McElderry's "The Climb", a quarter of Leona Lewis's "A Moment Like This", and a fifth of those of Matt Cardle's "When We Collide", Shayne Ward's "That's My Goal", James Arthur's "Impossible" and Alexandra Burke's "Hallelujah". The next fewest sales from a winner's song was Sam Bailey's version of "Skyscraper", which had first-week sales of 149,000 copies, 26,000 more than "Against All Odds". However, Louisa Johnson, Matt Terry and Rak Su would all have lower first week sales in later years.
